title: Opportunity Cost on a Commute
topic: Explain opportunity cost using a college student choosing among studying, commuting, and part-time work.

segments.text: I keep seeing opportunity cost in my econ notes, and it always sounds way more abstract than it probably is.
Picture tonight after your last lecture. You have two free hours before you get too tired, and you have to pick one plan.
If you take a two-hour part-time shift instead of reviewing for tomorrow's exam, your opportunity cost is the study boost you gave up.

left.label: 2 hrs Study
left.value: Stronger exam score, no extra pay tonight

right.label: 2 hrs Shift
right.value: Extra commute cash, less exam prep

segments.text: Wait, so even if studying at the library is free, choosing it still has a real cost?
Exactly. Economists look beyond cash on a receipt. Time and energy are scarce, so every choice crowds out another option.
One detail trips students up on exams: opportunity cost is only your single next-best option, not every possible thing you could do.

visualCue.title: Exam Rule to Remember
visualCue.explanation: Opportunity cost counts the single best alternative you gave up, not the sum of every unused option.

segments.text: That helps a lot. So my commute isn't just fare money—it's also the hour I could have used to rest or finish slides.
Right, unless you pair the commute with hands-free audio review, which shrinks what you sacrifice during transit.
Nice—look at the choice, spot the next-best trade-off, and that's opportunity cost in plain English.
